The Scissor-tailed flycatcher (Tyrannus forficatus) is a striking insectivore of the south-central United States and neighboring Mexico, whose life history has been characterized through field studies across its breeding range. At the typical body temperature of an active adult (41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]), the time from hatching to fledging is 15 days [tx = 15 days], a relatively rapid developmental period that reflects the high predation pressure typical of open grassland habitats. This species, like most passerines, exhibits altricial development; the altricial nestlings are entirely dependent on parental provisioning during this phase. The nestling period culminates in the achievement of sustained flight, at which point the fledgling leaves the nest. This rapid fledging period is somewhat shorter than that observed in some larger-bodied congeners from the genus Tyrannus, such as the Eastern Kingbird, and is likely an adaptation to maximize the probability of offspring survival in habitats where nest predation rates are high.

Comparative data from the closely related Eastern Kingbird (Tyrannus tyrannus) provide useful context for the incubation requirements of this genus, as direct measurements for the Scissor-tailed flycatcher are limited. The incubation period is followed by the hatching of altricial, blind, and nearly naked nestlings. This low neonatal body mass is typical of altricial passerines and is consistent with the substantial energetic investment required to incubate the calcareous eggs over the course of nearly two weeks. The rapid growth trajectory from this modest starting point is fueled by intensive biparental provisioning.

This ultimate wet weight is reached during the post-fledging period as juveniles continue to develop flight feather maturation and accumulate lipid reserves for migration. The species' comparatively slender body mass, in relation to its long, forked tail, is an adaptation for its aerial hawking foraging strategy. Body mass can fluctuate seasonally, with individuals often reaching their peak weight just prior to fall migration. The adult mass represents a roughly fifteen-fold increase over the neonatal mass of 2.8 grams [Wwb = 2.8 grams] recorded at hatching, highlighting the rapid growth trajectory during the nestling and juvenile periods.
